subject: Copywriting
subcategory: The Science of Storytelling in Ads
title: De Beers: A Diamond Is Forever
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: De Beers: A Diamond Is Forever.

hook.text: Before 1938, diamond engagement rings weren't tradition. De Beers invented the tradition with one sentence of copy.

buildup.text: Frances Gerety of N.W. Ayer wrote 'A Diamond Is Forever' in 1947. It linked diamonds permanently to eternal love.

discovery.text: The campaign planted the idea that a ring should cost two months' salary. A made-up rule that became sacred.

twist.text: Diamonds aren't rare. De Beers controlled supply and used copy to create artificial demand. The story was the product.

climax.text: One line of copy created a $72 billion industry. No other sentence in advertising history has generated more revenue.

punchline.text: One sentence invented a tradition and a $72 billion market.

quiz.question: When was 'A Diamond Is Forever' written?

details.summary: De Beers didn't just sell diamonds — they invented the cultural norm that diamonds are essential to engagements. The 'A Diamond Is Forever' campaign, running since 1947, is history's most successful example of storytelling that created an entirely new social ritual through advertising.
details.whyItMatters: De Beers demonstrates the ultimate power of brand storytelling: creating cultural norms that didn't previously exist. Understanding this campaign reveals how stories can reshape social behavior for generations.
takeaways: De Beers created the diamond engagement ring tradition through advertising
The campaign linked diamonds to eternal love, making them emotionally irreplaceable
Storytelling that becomes culture generates demand that no competitor can displace

faq.question: How did De Beers make diamonds a cultural necessity?
faq.answer: By systematically linking diamonds to love, commitment, and social status through decades of advertising. faq.question: Is A Diamond Is Forever the best slogan ever written?
faq.answer: AdAge named it the best slogan of the 20th century, and its impact is hard to dispute. Unlike most slogans that reinforce existing preferences, 'A Diamond Is Forever' created an entirely new consumer behavior — the expectation of diamond engagement rings — that persists nearly 80 years later.
